title: Haggai 2:1–9
context: Haggai’s second oracle is dated to the twenty-first day of the seventh month (2:1), less than a month after the work began. The LORD tells Haggai to speak to Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the remnant, and he addresses those who remember the house “in its former glory” and find the new one “as nothing” (2:3); compare Ezra 3:12, where older priests and leaders weep at the laying of the foundation. The LORD answers with “be strong”, “work, for I am with you”, and “Don’t be afraid” (2:4–5), and promises to shake the heavens, the earth, and all nations, so that “The treasure of all nations will come” and he will fill the house with glory (2:6–7). The silver and gold are his (2:8), and “The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former” (2:9). Hebrews 12:26–27 cites the shaking of 2:6 and applies it to a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Shared ground: both traditions read the passage as the LORD’s encouragement to discouraged builders, with the promises of 2 Samuel 7 about David’s house and the LORD’s house in the background.

verses.text: In the seventh month, in the twenty-first day of the month, the LORD’s word came by Haggai the prophet, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The date, “In the seventh month, in the twenty-first day of the month”, introduces a new oracle through Haggai the prophet. Arminian readers note that the LORD speaks again within weeks of the work beginning, meeting discouragement before it can halt the rebuilding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s timely care for his people in sending a fresh word as the work went on. Shared ground: both traditions read the dated heading as belonging to the oracle that follows, and as a reminder that the LORD’s word continued to sustain the people after their first obedience.

verses.text: “Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Haggai, “Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people”. Arminian readers note that the word is for leaders and people alike.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the whole covenant community addressed, from governor and high priest to the remnant. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the encouragement to follow is not reserved for leaders, and that the whole people share in the work and in the promise.

verses.text: ‘Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Isn’t it in your eyes as nothing?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory?” Arminian readers hear the LORD naming the people’s discouragement honestly, before answering it; compare Ezra 3:12, where some older people wept at the new foundation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD acknowledging that the new house seems “as nothing” in the eyes of those who remember the first. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the LORD does not dismiss the people’s disappointment, but meets it with the promises of 2:4–9.

verses.text: Yet now be strong, Zerubbabel,’ says the LORD. ‘Be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land,’ says the LORD, ‘and work, for I am with you,’ says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Yet now be strong, Zerubbabel,” and calls Joshua and “all you people of the land” to be strong and to “work, for I am with you”. Arminian readers hear encouragement that strengthens the people to keep working by grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s presence as the ground of the people’s strength, so that their work rests on his promise rather than their resources. Shared ground: both traditions read “I am with you” as the same promise given in 1:13, and the command to work as one the people can answer with courage.

verses.text: This is the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit lived among you. ‘Don’t be afraid.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD recalls “the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit lived among you.” Arminian readers hear the exodus covenant renewed as assurance, with the plain command, “Don’t be afraid”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s covenant faithfulness from the exodus onward, and many connect “my Spirit lived among you” with the LORD’s abiding presence among his people; compare Zechariah 4:6. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as grounding the call to courage in the LORD’s past and present faithfulness.

verses.text: For this is what the LORD of Armies says: ‘Yet once more, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says, “Yet once more, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land”. Arminian readers hear a promise that the LORD will act on a cosmic scale for his people, and they note that Hebrews 12:26–27 applies the words to a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s sovereign rule over heaven, earth, and nations, and they read Hebrews 12:26–27 as drawing out the final shaking that leaves only what “may remain”. Shared ground: both traditions read Haggai’s words in their own setting and also receive the use Hebrews makes of them, without merging the two.

verses.text: and I will shake all nations. The treasure of all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will shake all nations. The treasure of all nations will come”. Older English versions render the line as the desire of all nations, and many Christian readers, Arminian among them, have heard it messianically, as pointing to Christ. Others read it as the nations’ treasures, which fits 2:8.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise include both readings: a long line of Christian interpretation has heard the line as pointing to Christ, while many read it as the wealth of the nations brought to adorn the house, as 2:8 suggests. Shared ground: both traditions hold both readings, so the question does not divide them, and both hear the promise “I will fill this house with glory”.

verses.text: The silver is mine, and the gold is mine,’ says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine,” says the LORD of Armies. Arminian readers hear the LORD reassuring builders who lacked resources, since everything they need already belongs to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s ownership of all wealth, which he can bring to his house as he wills. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as answering the worry of 2:3 and as supporting the reading of 2:7 about the nations’ treasure, while resisting any reading that turns it into a promise of personal wealth.

verses.text: ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,’ says the LORD of Armies; ‘and in this place I will give peace,’ says the LORD of Armies.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,” says the LORD of Armies, who adds, “in this place I will give peace”. Arminian readers hear a promise beyond what the builders could see, which many Christians have read as fulfilled in Christ’s coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a promise of greater glory and peace, which many have read in the light of Christ and his presence among his people, holding that reading alongside the plain hope for the rebuilt temple. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise against the background of 2 Samuel 7 and the LORD’s commitment to David’s house and his own.
